hints: Focus on how strongly the tiny, highly charged $Al^{3+}$ ion distorts the electron cloud of chloride ions.
Recall what happens when anhydrous $AlCl_3$ hits water, and what the structure of the vapour dimer $Al_2Cl_6$ looks like.
Count how the two $AlCl_3$ units join together by chlorine lone pairs donating into empty orbitals on aluminium to complete octets.
walkthrough:
**Decide the true bonding type**

Think polarising power first. $Al^{3+}$ is very small and 3+, so it strongly polarises $Cl^-$.

That makes $AlCl_3$ covalent, not giant ionic, so it has a low melting point and sublimes around $180^{\circ}C$, much lower than ionic $MgCl_2$.

**Check the reaction with water**

Anhydrous $AlCl_3$ hydrolyses vigorously and fumes in moist air.

$$AlCl_3(s) + 3H_2O(l) \rightarrow Al(OH)_3(s) + 3HCl(aq)$$
The $HCl$ formed, plus further $[Al(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ acidity, gives a strongly acidic solution with pH well below 7, around pH 3.

**Picture the vapour dimer**

In the vapour, two $AlCl_3$ units join to form $Al_2Cl_6$ so each Al can achieve an octet.

Each Al starts with 3 covalent Al-Cl bonds. Two bridging Cl atoms each donate a lone pair into the empty orbital on the other Al, forming two coordinate (dative covalent) bonds, leaving four normal covalent terminal bonds.

options.A: False. Small $Al^{3+}$ does increase polarising power, but that makes bonding more covalent and melting point much lower, not higher. $AlCl_3$ sublimes easily while $MgCl_2$ is giant ionic with a high melting point near $714^{\circ}C$.
options.B: False. The reaction is vigorous but the product is acidic, not alkaline. Hydrolysis produces $HCl(aq)$ and the hexaaqua ion $[Al(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ releases $H^+$, so pH is less than 7, typically about 3.
options.C: Correct. $Al_2Cl_6$ has two Al centres bridged by two Cl atoms. There are four terminal Al-Cl covalent bonds plus two bridging Cl to Al coordinate bonds where both electrons come from Cl, giving two dative bonds per dimer.
options.D: False. Although Al and Cl differ in electronegativity, the very high charge density of $Al^{3+}$ polarises $Cl^-$ so strongly that the bond is substantially covalent. This is why $AlCl_3$ shows covalent properties like low melting point and dimer formation.
